title: Why pairing terms reveals the A.P. sum
subtitle: Arithmetic Progressions · Grade 10

beats.narration: How can we add a long arithmetic progression without counting every term? Let us discover a clever pattern.
Look at the five numbers: two, four, six, eight, and ten. The difference between neighboring terms is always two.
Start at the two ends. Two plus ten equals twelve. We can join the first and last terms into one pair.
Now move inward. Four plus eight also equals twelve. Both pairs have exactly the same sum.
Six is left in the middle. So the total is twelve plus twelve plus six, which equals thirty.
That pattern gives us a shortcut. The sum equals the number of terms, divided by two, multiplied by the first term plus the last term.
Here we have five terms. The first is two, and the last is ten. Five divided by two, times twelve, equals thirty. Exactly the same answer.
Your turn. What is the sum of three, six, nine, twelve, and fifteen? Think about the first and last terms. Pause here if you need more time.
There are five terms. Three plus fifteen is eighteen. Five divided by two, times eighteen, gives forty-five. Beautiful. You have just used the arithmetic progression sum formula.
